title: Rebuilding a portfolio so everything feels like one place

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A CV, a blog and a pile of project notes can feel like three different websites. Antoine's Hugo rebuild makes them feel like one.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How do you do that without making every page look identical?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A shared canvas, with different proportions per page. A slate-blue background and pale paper surface link everything, teal marks links and useful actions, and a serif font called Fraunces carries the titles. The CV puts his name, portrait and PDF button first. An article gets a comfortable reading column. A project note gets room for commands and diagrams.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Like one brand, three kinds of rooms.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Nice way to put it. Under the hood, the blog moved to a Hugo theme called Paper, and Antoine owns the overrides. Fix a template once and every article benefits. The header groups the kind of content, date, reading time and topics, and long articles get a collapsible table of contents.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Paired articles share a translation key, and a language switcher sits in the site header.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Repository notes live in their own section, so an article can follow one idea through the code while the note holds setup commands and references. The catalog has search and combinable filters, with separate buttons for documentation and GitHub.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Mermaid diagrams now start fitted to the space, with zoom, full size, fullscreen and SVG export. You can inspect one label without scrolling sideways.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How does he keep edits consistent?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: With repository skills, which are written rules for recurring changes. One knows the canonical CV pages, one knows the Hugo templates and bilingual bundles, and one defines how project notes are structured and what evidence a technical claim needs.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Everything stays in git. He builds the production site locally, checks light and dark mode, small and wide screens, language links and images, then publishes the static result.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the takeaway is one identity, many reading modes.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. The full write-up has the architecture diagram and the design notes.
